Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.
:::

## In 60 seconds

A deep network for the ECG is a stack of learned filters followed by a rule that turns scores into
probabilities. Trained on enough labeled recordings, such networks have matched or beaten
physicians on curated test sets: cardiologists for 12 rhythm classes on single-lead ambulatory
ECGs [@hannun2019], and cardiology residents for six abnormalities on 12-lead ECGs
[@ribeiro2020]. They can also find signals no reader uses, such as signs of **atrial fibrillation**
(AF, a fast, irregular rhythm of the upper chambers) in an ECG recorded during normal rhythm
[@attia2019]. Whether a model helps patients is a different question. Only prospective and
randomized studies answer it [@noseworthy2022; @yao2021; @adedinsewo2024]. This module builds a
classifier from its parts, shows what one output of a network can and cannot see, and shows why a
model that is excellent on its own test set can disappoint somewhere else.

## From the field

- **Labels set the ceiling.** In the 2017 PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge, experts
  relabeled the 1,129 recordings on which the best algorithms disagreed most. Their agreement was
  only fair, Fleiss' κ = 0.245 [@clifford2017]. A model cannot be more right than its labels; m35
  shows how to measure this ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)).
- **Bigger is not always better.** In the same Challenge, with 8,528 training recordings, a random
  forest on well-chosen features did as well as deep networks, and even the winning entries showed
  clear overtraining [@clifford2017].
- **The device is part of the data.** The Challenge recordings came from a handheld single-lead
  device at 300 Hz with a 0.5–40 Hz band, and many were inverted because users could hold the
  device either way round [@clifford2017]. PTB-XL holds 12-lead ECGs at 500 Hz, with a 100 Hz
  copy [@wagner2020]. A model moved between them meets a new sampling rate, band and polarity.
- **Split by patient.** PTB-XL's ten recommended folds keep every patient in one fold, with fold 10
  for testing and fold 9 for validation [@wagner2020]. A record-wise split leaks patients across
  sets ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-design-effect)).
- **Check subgroups.** A Stanford study trained a network on 12-lead ECGs from 326,518 patient
  encounters to predict heart failure within 5 years. Its performance fell with age, and it did
  significantly worse in Black patients aged 0 to 40 [@kaur2023].
- **Tools in practice.** A team from Stanford, UCSF and the device maker iRhythm Technologies
  trained an end-to-end network on 91,232 single-lead ECGs from 53,549 patients [@hannun2019]. Teams that cannot pool data use **federated
  learning**: each site trains locally and only model updates are shared. In one multinational
  study, whose authors included NVIDIA researchers, 20 institutes trained a model this way
  [@dayan2021]. NVIDIA FLARE is an open-source framework
  for such projects [@roth2022nvflare]. The course labs stay small and offline: NumPy and
  scikit-learn, with an optional PyTorch version.

## Derivations

Symbols: $x[n]$ an ECG sample, $f_s$ the sampling rate (Hz), $z_c$ the score for class $c$,
$p_c$ its probability, $y_c$ the label (1 for the true class, else 0), $w[k]$ a kernel weight,
$k_l$ and $s_l$ the kernel width and stride of layer $l$, $\pi$ prevalence, Se and Sp sensitivity
and specificity.

### From samples to class probabilities

A classifier maps a recording to one score per class. The **softmax** turns scores into
probabilities that are positive and sum to one:

$$
p_c = \frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_{j=1}^{C} e^{z_j}}
$$ {#eq-m37-softmax}

Training lowers the **cross-entropy** $L = -\sum_c y_c \log p_c$, the average surprise at the true
label. Its gradient with respect to the scores is short:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_c} = p_c - y_c
$$ {#eq-m37-ce-grad}

To derive it, write $\log p_c = z_c - \log \sum_j e^{z_j}$; then
$\partial L / \partial z_c = -y_c + \left(\sum_j y_j\right) p_c$, and the labels sum to one. Each
score moves in proportion to how wrong its probability was. Backpropagation carries this error
back through every layer.

With two classes, set the scores to $(0, u)$ and the softmax becomes the logistic function. This
is **logistic regression** when $u$ is a weighted sum of features $\mathbf x$:

$$
p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x), \qquad \sigma(u) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-u}}
$$ {#eq-m37-logistic}

**Key takeaways**

- Softmax makes probabilities; cross-entropy rewards putting probability on the true label.
- The error signal is $p - y$: a confident wrong answer gets the largest correction.
- Logistic regression is a one-layer network with two classes.

### Convolution is a learned filter

A convolutional layer slides a short kernel $w$ of width $K$ along the signal. Deep-learning
libraries compute a cross-correlation, with stride $s$ (the step between outputs) and bias $b$:

$$
y[n] = b + \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w[k]\, x[s n + k]
$$ {#eq-m37-conv}

This is a finite impulse response (FIR) filter, the same object as the digital filters of m04,
except that the weights are learned. Its gain at frequency $f$ follows from feeding it a
sinusoid:

$$
H(f) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w[k]\, e^{-i 2\pi f k / f_s}
$$ {#eq-m37-kernel-response}

A sinusoid comes out scaled by $\lvert H(f) \rvert$. A kernel $[1, 0, -1]/2$, for example, has
$\lvert H \rvert = \lvert \sin(2\pi f / f_s) \rvert$: a high-pass, derivative-like filter that
favors the steep QRS complex over the slow T wave.

Stacking layers widens what one output sees. With kernel widths $k_l$ and strides $s_l$, an
output of layer $L$ depends on

$$
r = 1 + \sum_{l=1}^{L} (k_l - 1) \prod_{j<l} s_j
$$ {#eq-m37-receptive-field}

input samples, its **receptive field**. Layer $l$ adds $k_l - 1$ samples, measured in steps of the
layers below it. In seconds, the receptive field is $r / f_s$.

::: {.demo #m37-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m37-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m37-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m37-d1-receptive-field.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- The receptive field is @eq-m37-receptive-field, exact for any stack of convolutions. The first
  layer has stride 1 and the others the chosen stride; all layers share one kernel width. Pooling,
  dilation and attention layers, which change the count, are not included.
- The trace is the course's synthetic ECG (approximate model, `labs/python/epml/aiecg.py`): a sum of
  Gaussian waves per beat, after the morphology part of @mcsharry2003. Its wave sizes, times and
  widths are illustrative, not reference values. It is noise-free and perfectly regular here.
- Heart rate, sampling rate and layer settings are illustrative inputs.
- What would change the result: a global pooling layer at the end lets the whole network see the
  whole record even when each output's receptive field is short.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A convolution kernel is a learned FIR filter; its frequency response is @eq-m37-kernel-response.
- One output sees only its receptive field. Strides grow it quickly, kernel width slowly.
- To judge whether beats come at irregular times, something in the network must see more than
  one interval between beats.

### What a rhythm model can measure

AF detectors look at one of two things: the atrial activity, or the ventricular response, that is,
the timing of the beats [@clifford2017]. Surface-ECG methods exist for both [@bollmann2006]. A
model can use either. The interval between two R peaks is the
**RR interval**. With $RR_i$ the $i$-th interval, $\overline{RR}$ its mean and $s_{RR}$ its sample
standard deviation, three simple features are

$$
\overline{RR}, \qquad
\mathrm{CV} = \frac{s_{RR}}{\overline{RR}}, \qquad
\mathrm{nRMSSD} = \frac{1}{\overline{RR}} \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \left(RR_{i+1} - RR_i\right)^2 }
$$ {#eq-m37-rr}

where $n$ is the number of intervals. CV measures spread; nRMSSD (normalized root mean square of
successive differences) measures beat-to-beat change. Regular beats give zero for both. Intervals
alternating between $a$ and $b$ give $\mathrm{nRMSSD} \cdot \overline{RR} = \lvert a - b \rvert$.
Finding the R peaks needs a QRS detector; the classic design band-passes, differentiates, squares
and integrates the signal before thresholding [@pan1985]. The lab uses a simplified version.

A model built on @eq-m37-rr and @eq-m37-logistic is small and easy to inspect. A convolutional
network learns its own features, which may include P-wave shape. The two can fail differently: an
irregular rhythm that is not AF (for example, frequent early beats) fools interval features, while
a different device or lead can fool a network trained on waveform shape. Many rhythms that are
not AF also have irregular intervals [@clifford2017].

**Key takeaways**

- Interval features are cheap, explainable and portable across devices.
- A network may rely on waveform shape you did not intend; test it where shape changes.
- In the Challenge data, simple features held their own against deep networks [@clifford2017].

### Hidden signals and the evidence ladder

Some networks find what no reader looks for. One trained on 10-second, 12-lead ECGs recorded in
normal sinus rhythm identified patients who had AF at other times, with an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI
0.86–0.88) on a held-out test set of 36,280 patients [@attia2019]. In the same test set, its F1
score was 39.2%. AUC does not depend on prevalence, but F1 and PPV do, and 8.4% of the test
patients had AF.

A good test-set result is the first rung of a ladder. Later rungs ask whether using the model
changes what happens:

| Rung | Example | What it showed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrospective test set | @attia2019 | The model ranks patients well on stored ECGs |
| Prospective, non-randomized | @noseworthy2022 | Over a mean 22.3 days of monitoring, AF was found in 7.6% of patients the model rated high risk and 1.6% of those rated low risk |
| Pragmatic randomized trial | @yao2021 | In 22,641 adults in primary care, giving clinicians the model's output raised new diagnoses of low ejection fraction from 1.6% to 2.1% |
| Pragmatic randomized trial | @adedinsewo2024 | In pregnant and postpartum women in Nigeria, AI-guided screening with a digital stethoscope found left ventricular dysfunction in 4.1% versus 2.0% with usual care; the 12-lead AI-ECG arm (3.4% versus 2.0%) did not reach significance |

When a model is used for screening, the burden falls on the confirmatory tests. For $N$ people
screened,

$$
N_{+} = N\left[\pi\,\mathrm{Se} + (1-\pi)(1-\mathrm{Sp})\right], \qquad
\frac{N_{+}}{N\pi\,\mathrm{Se}} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{PPV}}
$$ {#eq-m37-yield}

$N_+$ people are flagged, and each true case found costs $1/\mathrm{PPV}$ follow-up tests, with PPV
from [m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv).

::: {.demo #m37-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m37-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m37-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m37-d2-screening-yield.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Left: @eq-m37-yield with fixed sensitivity and specificity. Right: @eq-m37-prior-shift (next
  section), exact when the model's probabilities are calibrated where it was trained and the
  recordings of each class look the same in both places.
- Sensitivity, specificity and both prevalences are illustrative inputs, not values from a study.
- What would change the result: sensitivity and specificity themselves change with the population
  (spectrum effects), and calibrated probabilities are rare without checking ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-calibration)).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- AUC ranks; PPV and F1 depend on prevalence. Quote both.
- A screening model's cost is the follow-up it triggers: $1/\mathrm{PPV}$ tests per case found.
- Accuracy on stored ECGs is a first step. Benefit needs prospective, and ideally randomized,
  evidence.

### Moving a model to a new place

Data at a new site differ from training data in three main ways. The mix of classes changes
(**prior shift**). The recordings change: device, leads, sampling rate, filters, polarity,
population (**covariate shift**). Or the labels mean something different, for example a new
definition or a different reader (**concept shift**). Each needs its own check.

Prior shift has an exact fix when the recordings of each class look the same in both places. If a
calibrated model gives probability $p$ where the positive class had prevalence $\pi$, then where it
has prevalence $\pi'$ [@saerens2002]:

$$
p' = \frac{\dfrac{\pi'}{\pi}\, p}{\dfrac{\pi'}{\pi}\, p + \dfrac{1-\pi'}{1-\pi}\,(1-p)}
$$ {#eq-m37-prior-shift}

A model trained on balanced data ($\pi = 0.5$) and used where $\pi' = 0.02$ turns a raw 0.5 into
about 0.02. Ranking, and so AUC, does not change; thresholds and PPV do.

Covariate shift has no formula. It is found by testing on an **external** data set: one collected
elsewhere, never used for training or tuning (TRIPOD+AI, [@collins2024]). Practical checks for
ECG models: resample to a common rate, match the band, test with inverted polarity, and report
results by subgroup [@kaur2023]. Standards for digital ECG acquisition are set out by
Kligfield and colleagues [@kligfield2007].

**Key takeaways**

- Name the shift: prevalence, recordings or labels.
- Correct prevalence with @eq-m37-prior-shift; test everything else on external data.
- Report performance by subgroup, not only overall.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**AI-ECG to decide whom to monitor for AF.** In a prospective, non-randomized study, 1,003 patients
with stroke risk factors and no known AF wore a continuous monitor for up to 30 days after a
routine ECG [@noseworthy2022]. A network read the ECG and sorted patients into high and low risk.
AF was found in 48 of 633 high-risk patients (7.6%) and 6 of 370 low-risk patients (1.6%), an odds
ratio of 4.98 (95% CI 2.11–11.75). Compared with matched patients in usual care, AI-guided
screening was associated with more AF detected.

What this design shows, and what it does not, in the terms of this module:

- **It tests use, not only accuracy.** The model's output decided who was studied, a rung above
  the retrospective result it built on [@attia2019].
- **Its outcome is detection.** The primary outcome was newly diagnosed AF, not strokes prevented.
  A rise in detection is a reason to ask about outcomes, not an answer.
- **It was not randomized.** The comparison with usual care used propensity-score matching, which
  balances measured differences only. Randomized designs, such as the trial of @yao2021 for low
  ejection fraction, remove that concern.

Module m45 covers how such studies are designed and reported.

## How experts think

Before trusting an ECG model's number, ask:

1. **Who made the labels, and how much did they agree?** Fair agreement, as in the Challenge
   relabeling ($\kappa$ = 0.245, [@clifford2017]), caps any score.
2. **Was the split by patient?** If one patient's ECGs sit in both training and test sets, the
   score is optimistic ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-design-effect)).
3. **What can one output see?** Compute the receptive field (@eq-m37-receptive-field) and compare
   it with the feature you hope the model uses, such as successive RR intervals.
4. **Which numbers depend on prevalence?** AUC does not; PPV, F1 and the flags per case
   found (@eq-m37-yield) do.
5. **Was it tested somewhere else?** A different site, device, rate or population. Was the
   prevalence corrected (@eq-m37-prior-shift) and the subgroup performance reported [@kaur2023]?
6. **Which rung of evidence is this?** Retrospective accuracy, prospective use or a randomized
   trial [@attia2019; @noseworthy2022; @yao2021].

One sentence to keep: **a model's accuracy belongs to its test set; its usefulness belongs to the
place it is used.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Softmax (@eq-m37-softmax) | $p_c = e^{z_c} / \sum_j e^{z_j}$ |
| Cross-entropy gradient (@eq-m37-ce-grad) | $\partial L / \partial z_c = p_c - y_c$ |
| Logistic regression (@eq-m37-logistic) | $p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x)$ |
| Convolution layer (@eq-m37-conv) | $y[n] = b + \sum_k w[k]\, x[sn + k]$ |
| Kernel gain (@eq-m37-kernel-response) | $H(f) = \sum_k w[k]\, e^{-i2\pi fk/f_s}$ |
| Receptive field (@eq-m37-receptive-field) | $r = 1 + \sum_l (k_l - 1)\prod_{j<l} s_j$ samples, $r/f_s$ seconds |
| RR features (@eq-m37-rr) | $\overline{RR}$, $\mathrm{CV} = s_{RR}/\overline{RR}$, nRMSSD |
| Screening yield (@eq-m37-yield) | $N_+ = N[\pi\mathrm{Se} + (1-\pi)(1-\mathrm{Sp})]$; $1/\mathrm{PPV}$ flags per case |
| Prior shift (@eq-m37-prior-shift) | $p' \propto (\pi'/\pi)\,p$ against $((1-\pi')/(1-\pi))(1-p)$ |

**Two data sets used in the lab**

| | PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017 [@clifford2017] | PTB-XL [@wagner2020] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leads | One (lead I equivalent, often inverted) | 12 |
| Sampling | 300 Hz, 0.5–40 Hz band | 500 Hz, plus a 100 Hz copy |
| Length | 9–61 s | 10 s |
| Size | 8,528 public training recordings | 21,837 records from 18,885 patients (paper) |
| Labels | Normal, AF, other rhythm, noisy | 71 statements, multi-label |
| Splits | Hidden test set | Ten folds by patient; fold 10 for testing |

**Rules of thumb**

- Report AUC with PPV at the prevalence of use, and calibration.
- Count receptive fields in seconds and in beats.
- Split by patient; test on an external site; report subgroups.
- Retrospective accuracy is not clinical benefit.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Derive the gradient of the softmax cross-entropy with respect to the scores.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With $\log p_c = z_c - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$, the loss is
$L = -\sum_c y_c z_c + \left(\sum_c y_c\right)\log \sum_j e^{z_j}$. Differentiating,
$\partial L/\partial z_c = -y_c + \left(\sum_c y_c\right) e^{z_c}/\sum_j e^{z_j} = p_c - y_c$, because
one-hot labels sum to one (@eq-m37-ce-grad). The error is the gap between predicted and true
probability, so a confident wrong prediction gets the largest update.

</details>

**Q2. Why is a convolutional layer "just a filter", and what does that buy an engineer?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Each output is a weighted sum of a short window of inputs (@eq-m37-conv): an FIR filter with
learned weights. Its frequency response (@eq-m37-kernel-response) can be computed and plotted like
any filter. That lets you check what a trained first layer passes (QRS energy, baseline wander,
mains interference) and reason about sampling-rate changes: a kernel learned at 300 Hz has a
different response in hertz when applied at 500 Hz.

</details>

**Q3. A network has four layers of width 9; the last three have stride 2. At 100 Hz and 70 bpm,
how many RR intervals does one output see?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$r = 1 + 8(1 + 1 + 2 + 4) = 65$ samples (@eq-m37-receptive-field), or 0.65 s. One RR interval at
70 bpm lasts about 0.86 s, so an output sees less than one interval. On its own it cannot compare
successive beats; the network can judge irregularity only after a pooling or later stage combines
outputs (demo m37-d1).

</details>

**Q4. Your model's AUC is 0.87, but its F1 is 39%. Is something wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not necessarily. AUC measures ranking and does not depend on prevalence; F1 combines sensitivity
with PPV, and PPV falls when positives are rare. @attia2019 reported exactly this pair, with 8.4%
of test patients positive. Report both, and give PPV at the prevalence where the model will be
used (@eq-m37-yield).

</details>

**Q5. A model trained on balanced data outputs 0.5 for a new patient. In the clinic, prevalence is
2%. What probability should be shown?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

If the model is calibrated on its training data and each class's recordings look the same in the
clinic, @eq-m37-prior-shift with $\pi = 0.5$ and $\pi' = 0.02$ gives
$p' = 0.02 \cdot 0.5 / (0.02 \cdot 0.5 + 0.98 \cdot 0.5) = 0.02$. The ranking is unchanged, so AUC
stays the same, but a threshold of 0.5 now flags far too many people. Check calibration on local
data before trusting either number.

</details>

**Q6. Name three ways a single-lead handheld ECG differs from a 12-lead resting ECG, and how each
could break a model.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Sampling and band: the Challenge data are 300 Hz with a 0.5–40 Hz band [@clifford2017], while
PTB-XL is 500 Hz with a 100 Hz copy [@wagner2020], so learned filters see different frequencies.
Polarity: many handheld recordings are inverted, so a model keyed to an upright R wave fails.
Population and length: self-recorded 9–61 s strips versus 10-s clinical ECGs change the mix of
rhythms, noise and duration. Fixes: resample, match the band, augment with inverted signals, and
test externally.

</details>

**Q7. Why might a random forest on RR features match a deep network on AF detection?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

AF's main surface signs, irregular intervals and missing organized P waves, can be summarized by a
few features (@eq-m37-rr). With limited training data, a model with few, well-chosen inputs has
less room to overfit. In the 2017 Challenge, with 8,528 training recordings, that is what happened
[@clifford2017]. Deep networks gain when data are larger or the signal is subtler, as with AF
signatures in sinus-rhythm ECGs [@attia2019].

</details>

**Q8. What is wrong with splitting ECG records at random into training and test sets?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Patients with several records end up on both sides. The model can recognize the person, not the
rhythm, and the test score is optimistic. Split by patient, as PTB-XL's folds do [@wagner2020],
and use the design effect from [m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-design-effect) to judge how
many independent cases you really have.

</details>

**Q9. A study shows that an AI-ECG increases AF detection. A manager concludes it prevents strokes.
Respond.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Detection is an intermediate outcome. The study cited for this, @noseworthy2022, measured newly
diagnosed AF, not strokes, and was not randomized: its comparison with usual care used propensity
matching. Stroke prevention needs a trial with that outcome. The evidence ladder in this module
separates "the model ranks well", "using it changes what clinicians find" and "patients do
better".

</details>

**Q10. Your model works overall but worse in one age group. What do you check and what can you
change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Check the number of cases in the subgroup (small groups give wide intervals), label quality, and
whether the subgroup's recordings differ (device, setting). In @kaur2023, performance fell with age
and was significantly worse in young Black patients. Adding demographics to the model or
rebalancing data did not fix it, while thresholds chosen per subgroup improved F1. Report
subgroups, with confidence intervals, and decide thresholds openly.

</details>

**Q11. What is federated learning, and what problem does it not solve?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Each site trains on its own data and shares only model updates, so raw recordings stay local
[@dayan2021; @roth2022nvflare]. It eases data sharing and can improve how well a model generalizes
across sites. It does not fix label disagreement, differences in label definitions between sites,
or the need to test on a site that took no part in training.

</details>

**Q12. How would you design a first external validation for an AF detector trained on handheld
single-lead data?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Pick a data set from another source with patient-level splits, for example lead I of PTB-XL's
fold 10 [@wagner2020]. Freeze the model and its threshold before looking. Harmonize sampling rate
and band; report AUC, sensitivity and specificity at the frozen threshold, calibration, and PPV
after correcting for prevalence (@eq-m37-prior-shift). State the differences that remain (lead,
setting, population). The lab does this in part E.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds an ECG classifier from its parts and then moves it to a new data set. It runs in
about two minutes, including downloads.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Check the softmax gradient (@eq-m37-ce-grad) numerically; plot a kernel's frequency response (@eq-m37-kernel-response) | synthetic |
| B | Check @eq-m37-receptive-field by perturbing inputs; count beats per output | synthetic |
| C | Build a synthetic cohort with several records per patient; compare record-wise and patient-wise splits with RR features (@eq-m37-rr) and logistic regression | synthetic |
| D | Train a small convolutional network written in NumPy; test both models on inverted signals and on irregular rhythms that are not AF | synthetic |
| E | Train on the Challenge 2017 data, test unchanged on PTB-XL lead I; correct for prevalence (@eq-m37-prior-shift) | PhysioNet |
| F | Optional: the same network in PyTorch | synthetic |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m37_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m37_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m37_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part E:** small subsets of the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017 training set
  [@cinc2017data; @clifford2017] (Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0) and of PTB-XL 1.0.3
  [@ptbxl103; @wagner2020] (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0), downloaded from PhysioNet and
  checked against each database's published SHA-256 checksums [@goldberger2000]. Without internet
  access, part E is skipped.
- **Part F** runs only if PyTorch is installed (`pip install torch`); otherwise it is skipped.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A single layer has kernel width 31 at 300 Hz. How long a stretch of ECG does one output
see?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

31 samples (@eq-m37-receptive-field with one layer), or about 0.10 s.

</details>

**S2. True or false: correcting for a new prevalence with @eq-m37-prior-shift changes a model's
AUC.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. The correction is a monotone function of $p$, so the ranking of patients, and therefore AUC,
is unchanged. Thresholds, PPV and calibration change.

</details>

**S3. Sensitivity 0.8, specificity 0.9, prevalence 2%. About how many people are flagged per 1,000
screened, and how many flags per true case?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$N_+ = 1000(0.02 \cdot 0.8 + 0.98 \cdot 0.1) = 16 + 98 = 114$ flagged, 16 true cases, so about 7
flags per case found (@eq-m37-yield; demo m37-d2 defaults).

</details>

**S4. RR intervals alternate 0.6 s, 1.0 s, 0.6 s, 1.0 s, … What is nRMSSD?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Successive differences are all 0.4 s, so RMSSD = 0.4 s; the mean is 0.8 s; so nRMSSD
= 0.5 (@eq-m37-rr).

</details>

**S5. Which rung of the evidence ladder is a cluster-randomized trial in which clinicians do or do
not see the model's output?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

A pragmatic randomized trial: it tests whether using the model changes what happens, as in the
trial of @yao2021.

</details>

**S6. Why does doubling the stride of every layer after the first grow the receptive field faster
than doubling the kernel width of one layer?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

In @eq-m37-receptive-field each layer's $k_l - 1$ is multiplied by the product of all earlier
strides, so strides compound across layers, while one wider kernel adds only once.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Network against cardiologists.** Hannun and colleagues, Figure 1 and Table 1 [@hannun2019;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6784839/)]. ROC curves for the network
  and F1 scores for the network and for six cardiologists, against a committee consensus. A
  publisher correction notes that the x axis of Figure 1a is 1 − specificity. Compare where the
  network and the average cardiologist fall for AF. This module: @eq-m37-softmax, interview Q4.
- **Confusion matrices.** Hannun and colleagues, Figure 2 [@hannun2019]. Which rhythm classes the
  network and the averaged cardiologists confuse; the correction notes that panel b is for the
  cardiologists. Both tend to struggle with the same classes, a sign that the labels themselves are
  hard (From the field).
- **A data set built for testing.** Wagner and colleagues, the overview figure and the description
  of the cross-validation folds [@wagner2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248071/)].
  Look at how folds are assigned by patient and why fold 10 holds only human-validated records.
  This module: interview Q8 and Q12.
- **Overtraining in a public challenge.** Clifford and colleagues, the table of top-scoring entries
  with their training, validation and test scores [@clifford2017;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5978770/)]. Compare each entry's
  training score with its test score. This module: From the field, interview Q7.

## Further reading

- **Overviews.** @svennberg2025: the 2025 EHRA, HRS and ESC statement on the state of AI in
  clinical EP. @feeny2020: a review of AI and machine learning in arrhythmias and cardiac EP,
  written for readers new to the methods.
- **Data sets.** @wagner2020 and @clifford2017, with their PhysioNet pages
  [@ptbxl103; @cinc2017data].
- **Evidence.** @attia2019, @noseworthy2022, @yao2021 and @adedinsewo2024 form a ladder from
  retrospective accuracy to randomized trials.
- **ECG technology.** @kligfield2007: how the digital ECG is acquired and processed.
- **Methods.** @saerens2002 on prior shift; @collins2024 (TRIPOD+AI) on reporting prediction
  models; [m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd) for validation basics.
- **Training across sites.** @dayan2021 and @roth2022nvflare on federated learning.
